chunks: LDO trade-offs vs step-down regulators. The question: What are some tradeoffs of LDOs compared to other stepdown regulators?
An LDO is simple and quiet, but it wastes the whole voltage difference as heat. A buck converter is efficient, but needs an inductor and makes switching ripple and noise.
So the choice depends on headroom and current. With a small headroom or a small load, or when the supply feeds sensitive parts such as sensors or audio circuits, use an LDO.
With a big headroom and more than a few hundred milliamps, use a buck.
Slowing a car by braking turns all the extra motion into heat, like an LDO. Slowing it with regenerative braking gets some energy back, like a buck.
Plain brakes are simple and smooth, but they waste energy and get hot. Regenerative braking saves energy but adds machinery and some noise.
The analogy skips the fact that you can combine them: a buck first, then an LDO to clean up.

54 amps at 70 degrees Celsius ambient, and a 200 degrees Celsius/W package to about 0. 16 amps, regardless of the transistor's current rating. At 12 volts to 3. 3 volts (8.
7 volts headroom) the 60 degrees Celsius/W part can only give about 0. 1 amps. A buck's heat is the small loss I outV out(1 over -1) , so it is not limited the same way.

Efficiency: output power divided by input power ("LDO meaning and dropout advantage"). Headroom: the difference between input and output voltage.
Ripple and EMI: the switching noise a buck makes and an LDO does not. EMI (electromagnetic interference) is the part that spreads to nearby circuits.
PSRR: how well a regulator blocks noise from its input. Quiescent current: the current a regulator uses just to stay on.
Take 12 volts in, 3. 3 volts out, and a 1 amps load. The LDO wastes (12-3. 3) times 1 equals 8. 7 watts, an efficiency of about 27%. A 90% buck wastes only about 3. 3 over 0. 9-3.
3 about 0. 37 watts. Now take 3. 5 volts in instead. The LDO wastes just (3. 5-3. 3) times 1 equals 0. 2 watts, and it needs no inductor, so the LDO wins. That is the whole idea.
"LDOs are simple, quiet and small, with fast transient response and no EMI, but their efficiency is V out over V in and the lost power is heat, so they only work at small headroom or low current.
Buck converters are efficient at large step-downs and high currents but need an inductor, make switching noise and EMI, and cost more area.
So: small headroom or sensitive analog, LDO; big headroom or high current, buck; and if you need both, buck followed by an LDO."
